parole.significato: Independent research, observation of something (as opposed to second hand accounts)
parole.testo: From New Latin autopsia, from Ancient Greek αὐτοψῐ́ᾱ (autopsĭ́ā, “seeing with one's own eyes”).

parole.significato: alphabet (an ordered set of letters used in a language), especially the Latin alphabet.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin alphabētum (“alphabet”), from Ancient Greek ἀλφάβητος (alphábētos), from ἄλφα (álpha, “alpha”) and βήτα (bḗta, “beta”) (the names of the first two letters in the Greek alphabet). Doublet of алфа́ві́т (alfávít). Compare Ukrainian алфабет (alfabet) (1627), алфабетумъ (alfabetum) (1

Borrowed from Latin angina, derived from Ancient Greek ἀγχόνη (ankhónē, “strangling”).

parole.significato: Arachis (genus within the family Fabaceae – flowering plants, of which the peanut is the best known)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from New Latin arachis, from Ancient Greek (see ἄρακος (árakos), ἀράχιδνα (arákhidna)). Compare Russian ара́хис (aráxis).
Ultimately from Latin architectūra, from Ancient Greek ἀρχιτέκτων (arkhitéktōn). Cognate with Russian архитекту́ра (arxitektúra), Belarusian архітэкту́ра (arxitektúra), Polish architektura.
Borrowed from Latin astronomus, from Ancient Greek ἀστρονόμος (astronómos).

Derived via Western European languages from Latin atrophia, from Ancient Greek ἀτροφία (atrophía, “a wasting away”), from ἄτροφος (átrophos, “ill-fed, un-nourished”). Compare Russian атрофи́я (atrofíja), Belarusian атрафі́я (atrafíja), Polish atrofia.

parole.significato: aura (the distinctive atmosphere or quality associated with someone or something)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin aura (“a breeze, a breath of air, the air”).

Derived via Western European languages from Late Latin basaltes, a misspelling of Latin basanites, from Ancient Greek βασανίτης (basanítēs), from βάσανος (básanos, “touchstone”).
From Latin bacterium, from Ancient Greek βακτήριον (baktḗrion). Compare Russian бакте́рия (baktérija), Belarusian бактэ́рыя (baktéryja), Polish bakteria.
From Latin bronchia + New Latin -ītis, from Ancient Greek βρόγχος (brónkhos) + -ῖτις (-îtis). Compare Russian бронхи́т (bronxít), Belarusian бранхі́т (branxít).
Ultimately from Latin harmonia, from Ancient Greek ἁρμονία (harmonía, “joint, union, agreement, concord of sounds”). Compare Russian гармо́ния (garmónija).

From Late Latin genealogia, from Ancient Greek γενεαλογία (genealogía), from γενεά (geneá, “generation, descent”), with -ло́гія (-lóhija) ending from Ancient Greek -λογία (-logía). Compare Russian генеало́гия (genealógija), Belarusian генеало́гія (hjenjealóhija), Polish genealogia.

Borrowed from Latin glossārium, from Ancient Greek γλῶσσα (glôssa, “tongue”).

From New Latin hygiena, from Ancient Greek ὑγιεινή (hugieinḗ). Compare Russian гигие́на (gigijéna), Belarusian гігіе́на (hihijéna), Polish higiena.
From Late Latin hippocampus, from Ancient Greek ἱππόκαμπος (hippókampos). Compare Russian гиппока́мп (gippokámp), Polish hipokamp.
Borrowed from Latin hippopotamus, from Ancient Greek ἱπποπόταμος (hippopótamos).

Borrowed from Late Latin dilemma, from Ancient Greek δίλημμα (dílēmma, “ambiguous proposition”), from δι- (di-, “having two of”) + λῆμμα (lêmma, “premise, proposition”). Compare Russian диле́мма (dilémma), Belarusian дыле́ма (dyljéma).
Derived via Western European languages from Late Latin dosis, from Ancient Greek δόσῐς (dósĭs).

Derived via Western European languages from Latin diabētēs, from Ancient Greek διαβήτης (diabḗtēs). Compare Russian диабе́т (diabét), Belarusian дыябе́т (dyjabjét).

parole.significato: range of problems, agenda, subject matter

From New Latin psychosis, from Ancient Greek ψυχή (psukhḗ, “vital spirit, soul”) + -ωσις (-ōsis, “state, abnormal condition, or action”).

From Latin pȳramis, pȳramidis, from Ancient Greek πῡραμίς (pūramís), πῡραμίδος (pūramídos). Compare Russian пирами́да (piramída), Polish piramida.

From New Latin spora, from Ancient Greek σπορά (sporá, “sowing, seed”).

parole.significato: troglodyte (a member of a supposed prehistoric race that lived in caves or holes, a caveman)
